title: Programming Paradigms
relevance: Interviewers ask this to check whether candidates understand why OOP exists—grouping data with the operations on it—before diving into language features.

phases.goal: Establish what a programming paradigm is and that the four stages grow structure to manage complexity.

must_hit.point: A programming paradigm is a style of organising code.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate defines paradigm as an organisational style of code, not as a language or syntax feature.

must_hit.point: Paradigm history is about managing growing complexity: each stage keeps the previous capabilities and adds a new way of grouping related things.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says later styles build on earlier ones and add grouping so large programs stay comprehensible.

must_hit.point: Four stages mark the evolution and are read left to right as increasing structure: monolithic, procedural/modular, modular with structures, then object-oriented.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the four stages in order and frames them as increasing structure.

probes: What is a programming paradigm, and why did these styles evolve?

hints.1: Think about what a paradigm organises—not which language you use.
hints.2: The story is managing complexity by grouping related things into larger units.
hints.3: Define paradigm as a style of organising code, then list the four stages from monolithic through OOP as increasing structure.

phases.goal: Show how each stage groups code differently—from one block, to functions, to structures-plus-functions, to a class.

must_hit.point: Monolithic programs are one undivided block of statements with no named functions or structures to group data; that works only for very small programs.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes a single undivided program with no reusable units and limits it to very small programs.

must_hit.point: Procedural/modular (C style) packages actions into named callable functions that main invokes in sequence, while data still lives loosely apart from those functions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions functions and main calling them, and that data and functions remain separate.

must_hit.point: Modular with structures bundles related fields into a structure passed to functions, so related data travels together, but functions stay defined separately from that data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes a structure of related fields passed into functions, with behaviour still outside the data.

must_hit.point: Object-oriented style uses a class that binds both the data and the functions that operate on it; main creates objects and calls functions through the object, encapsulating state and behaviour.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says class unifies data and functions, objects are created, and calls go through the object (encapsulation).

probes: Walk through how code organisation changes from a monolithic program to an object-oriented class.
In the structure-based style, what still remains separate even after related fields are bundled?

hints.1: Start with one undivided block, then add functions, then group data, then fuse both.
hints.2: Contrast where data lives versus where the functions that use it are defined at each stage.
hints.3: Monolith: one block. Procedural: named functions, data loose. Structures: Info passed in, functions still separate. OOP: class Info holds data and functions; call via an object.

phases.goal: Explain what each step gains in grouping and what prior styles still leave apart.

must_hit.point: Procedural style separates what is done into named units, but still keeps data and the functions that operate on it apart.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Credits functions for packaging actions, then notes data and behaviour remain split.

must_hit.point: Structures improve cohesion of related data travelling together, but still leave functions defined separately from the data they act on.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says structures help data travel together without yet uniting behaviour with that data.

must_hit.point: Object orientation fuses those halves so code is organised around the things (objects) in the problem rather than a flat list of procedures.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts organising around objects/things versus a flat procedure list, with data and behaviour together.

probes: What problem does moving from plain functions to structures solve, and what does it still not solve?
Why is a class a larger answer to 'what belongs together?' than a structure alone?

hints.1: Ask what each stage groups—and what it still leaves split.
hints.2: Functions group actions; structures group fields; only a class groups both.
hints.3: Structures let related data travel together but keep functions outside; a class encapsulates data and operations and centres design on objects.

phases.goal: Connect the progression to how OOP is used in main and to the guiding grouping intuition.

must_hit.point: In OOP, main creates objects of a class and invokes the class's functions through those objects.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes creating an object and calling member functions on it rather than free functions alone.

must_hit.point: The guiding intuition is grouping: each paradigm answers 'what belongs together?' with a larger, more meaningful unit, culminating in the object that keeps state and operations on that state in one place.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the grouping question and that the object is the unit that co-locates state and its operations.

probes: If you were explaining OOP on a whiteboard after showing C-style structs, what would you draw next and why?
How does the 'what belongs together?' question change as you move from functions to structures to objects?

hints.1: Picture main creating something and calling behaviour on that something.
hints.2: The last step is not more data fields—it is putting operations inside the same unit as the data.
hints.3: Draw class Info with fields and functions together; in main, Info i; then i.function1()—state and operations in one place.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Functions package what is done into named callable units, but data stays loose; structures bundle related fields so that data travels together as one argument, without yet attaching the functions to that data.

With structures, related data is grouped but functions remain separate; a class fuses data and the functions that operate on it into one encapsulated unit, so design centres on objects rather than a flat list of procedures.

tradeoffs.topic: Monolithic program vs procedural modular style
tradeoffs.strong_answer: A monolithic program is one undivided block with no reusable named units and only suits very small programs; procedural style breaks logic into named functions that main invokes in sequence.

gotchas.trap: Treating a C-style structure plus free functions as already object-oriented.
gotchas.correction: Structures only bundle related data fields; the functions that act on them are still defined separately. OOP requires a class that binds data and those functions together and calls them through an object.

gotchas.trap: Thinking each new paradigm discards the previous style's capabilities.
gotchas.correction: Each paradigm keeps the previous one's capabilities and adds a new way of grouping related things so larger programs stay comprehensible.

gotchas.trap: Describing OOP only as 'using classes' without the grouping motivation.
gotchas.correction: The point of the progression is answering 'what belongs together?' with a larger unit—culminating in an object that keeps state and the operations on that state in one place (encapsulation).
